claims.text: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a duplex FCC and BCC/intermetallic lamellar microstructure.
The as-cast microstructure is coarse and has comparatively low dislocation and twin densities.
AlCoCrFeNi2.1 can be processed by cryogenic rolling followed by annealing.
The annealing step following cryogenic rolling should specifically be a low-temperature anneal.
Cryogenic rolling followed by annealing will produce an ultrafine duplex microstructure while retaining or refining the lamellar architecture.
The processing route will increase the density of nanoscale twins within the FCC phase.
Cryogenic rolling substantially increases dislocation density.
Cryogenic rolling activates deformation twinning in this alloy.
Low-temperature annealing relieves residual stresses while stabilizing deformation-generated dislocations and twins.
Appropriate low-temperature annealing can avoid significant grain or lamellar coarsening.
Hierarchical refinement and nanotwinning enhance work hardening.
Enhanced work hardening delays necking and thereby improves ductility while retaining high strength.
Cryogenic rolling and annealing can increase the strength of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 relative to the as-cast alloy.
The processed alloy should attain a yield strength near or above 1.2 GPa.
Cryogenic rolling and annealing will maintain or improve ductility relative to the as-cast baseline.
AlCoCrFeNi2.1 has been reported at approximately 944 MPa strength and 25.6% ductility, while cryogenic rolling and annealing produced approximately 1.47 GPa strength and 14% ductility.
Tailored thermomechanical processing has previously produced an ultrafine duplex AlCoCrFeNi2.1 microstructure that inherits the cast lamellar architecture and improves its mechanical response.
Excessive annealing or substantially different deformation and temperature parameters may eliminate the beneficial refinement.
The proposed benefit may be limited to EHEAs possessing an inherent eutectic lamellar architecture.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis and falsification rule require an increase in ductility, whereas the predicted outcome allows ductility merely to be maintained. A result with increased strength and unchanged ductility would therefore satisfy the predicted outcome but not the stronger simultaneous-increase criterion.
The route is described as a single intervention, but it consists of two distinct sequential processing operations: cryogenic rolling and annealing.
